iglesia_ni_cristo.trinity:
Members of the Iglesia ni Cristo confess one God, the Father alone. Jesus Christ is honored as Lord, Savior and the one mediator between God and humanity, but is taught to be a man chosen and sent by God, not God himself. The Holy Spirit is understood as the power or work of God and not as a separate person.

Members hold that the doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Bible and entered Christianity after the apostolic age. They ground their own teaching in biblical passages that speak of the Father as the only true God. Most other Christian traditions disagree with this account of Jesus and the Spirit, and members are aware of that, but they present their teaching as a return to what Scripture says plainly.
iglesia_ni_cristo.one_true_church:
The Iglesia ni Cristo, which means Church of Christ, teaches that Christ founded one church and that this church is necessary for salvation. Members understand the New Testament to describe a single body that Christ purchased with his own blood, not a collection of equal denominations.

They teach that the church established by the apostles fell into apostasy after the apostolic age, and that God restored the true church in the last days. Because of this, members regard salvation as found within the Church of Christ. The emphasis is on unity of doctrine and on obedience to what members read as the plain teaching of Scripture. Other Christian traditions generally do not accept this understanding, and members are used to being asked about it.
iglesia_ni_cristo.true_church_claim:
Members of the Iglesia ni Cristo believe that their church is the true Church of Christ described in the New Testament, restored in 1914 in the Philippines through Felix Manalo, whom they regard as God's last messenger. They point to the name Church of Christ, which they read in the New Testament, and to biblical prophecies which they believe were fulfilled in the church's rise.

The church is led by an Executive Minister and has a structured process of doctrinal instruction before baptism and membership. Members see the claim as a matter of faithfulness to God's word, not of pride. Other Christians generally do not accept this claim, and it is one reason why relationships with other churches are limited, since members believe that joining the true church is a step of obedience.
